first_check.explanation: This general description is supported. Title VIII of SOX (§ 802) added 18 U.S.C. § 1519, which criminalizes destroying or falsifying records to obstruct federal matters and applies to 'whoever', including public-company personnel. It also added § 1520 on retention of audit records. § 1520(c) says other federal and state duties to maintain documents still apply. Taken together, SOX does impose significant retention and preservation obligations in the public-company context, though some of them (e.g., § 1520) fall on auditors rather than on the issuer itself.

citations.cited_for: Imposes specific retention requirements for certain categories of records
citations.context: Additionally, SEC Rule 17a-4 and other regulatory provisions impose specific retention requirements applicable to certain categories of records maintained by publicly traded companies and their affiliates.

first_check.explanation: Rule 17a-4 is a record-preservation rule for exchange members, brokers, and dealers (and certain security-based swap entities that are registered broker-dealers). It does not set retention requirements for records kept by publicly traded companies in general. Nexfield is a NASDAQ-listed industrial company, not a broker-dealer. Describing 17a-4 as imposing retention requirements on "records maintained by publicly traded companies and their affiliates" misstates who the rule covers. A broker-dealer affiliate would be covered only because it is a broker-dealer, not because it is affiliated with a public company.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: "§ 240.17a-4 Records to be preserved by certain exchange members, brokers and dealers." ... "Every member, broker or dealer subject to § 240.17a-3 must preserve for a period of not less than 6 years..."

second_check.explanation: The finding holds after a search for supporting text. 17 C.F.R. § 240.17a-4 applies only to securities-industry intermediaries. Paragraphs (a) and (b) each begin "Every member, broker or dealer subject to § 240.17a-3 must preserve...", and the rule's scope covers exchange members, brokers and dealers, registered broker-dealers, and security-based swap dealers or participants that are registered broker-dealers. Nothing in it extends the requirements to issuers or to public companies generally. The retention policy (nexfield-retention-policy.docx.md, para. 2) says Rule 17a-4 imposes "specific retention requirements applicable to certain categories of records maintained by publicly traded companies and their affiliates." That sentence is part of a passage listing the obligations Nexfield, a NASDAQ-listed industrial company, is subject to as a public company. The words "certain categories" and "affiliates" do not save it. A broker-dealer affiliate would be covered because it is a broker-dealer, not because it belongs to a public-company group, and the documents give no sign that Nexfield has a broker-dealer affiliate. The policy therefore misstates who the rule covers. The citation itself (SEC Rule 17a-4) is correct and the rule is real, so MISCHARACTERIZED is the right status.

first_check.correct_citation: Araujo v. N.J. Transit Rail Operations, Inc., 708 F.3d 152, 160-62 (3d Cir. 2013)
first_check.explanation: The case is real and the citation is correct (3d Cir., Feb. 19, 2013). It arose under the Federal Railroad Safety Act's contributing-factor framework, not SOX. At 160-62 the court held that temporal proximity (disciplinary charges filed 'a few days after' the injury report), together with evidence of disparate treatment, was enough to make a prima facie case, while calling that evidence 'not overwhelming.' The court did not state a general rule that 'days or weeks' is sufficient. The parenthetical generalizes the holding, and the discussion runs from 160 to 162 rather than sitting only on 161. Still, the case reasonably supports the point that a gap of days can support a prima facie showing of causation.

citations.cited_for: Punitive damages demanded for reckless disregard of rights under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act
citations.context: Nexfield's conduct was willful, malicious, and undertaken with reckless disregard for Mr. Kovach's federally protected rights under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.

first_check.correct_citation: Sarbanes-Oxley Act § 806, 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(c)
first_check.explanation: The letter demands punitive damages for reckless disregard of rights under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. SOX § 806's remedies provision limits relief to making the employee whole: reinstatement, back pay with interest, and special damages including litigation costs, expert fees and attorney fees. It does not authorize punitive damages, and courts have struck SOX punitive damages demands (e.g., Hanna v. WCI Communities, 348 F. Supp. 2d 1332, 1333 (S.D. Fla. 2004), where the plaintiff conceded they are unavailable). The "reckless disregard of federally protected rights" standard comes from 42 U.S.C. § 1981a, not SOX. The letter's own remedies paragraph (Section V.A) lists only make-whole relief. Punitive damages might be pursued under the separate Texas common-law claim, but the demand rests them on SOX.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: An employee prevailing in any action under subsection (b)(1) shall be entitled to all relief necessary to make the employee whole. Relief ... shall include--(A) reinstatement ... (B) the amount of back pay, with interest; and (C) compensation for any special damages ... / Mr. Hanna's response concedes that punitive damages are unavailable under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. The remedies provision of SOX § 806, 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(c), reads: "(1) An employee prevailing in any action under subsection (b)(1) shall be entitled to all relief necessary to make the employee whole. (2) Relief ... shall include--(A) reinstatement ...; (B) the amount of back pay, with interest; and (C) compensation for any special damages sustained as a result of the discrimination, including litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorney fees." It does not mention punitive damages. Hanna v. WCI Communities, Inc., 348 F. Supp. 2d 1332, 1333 (S.D. Fla. 2004) (CourtListener opinion 2306416) supports the first reviewer: "Mr. Hanna's response concedes that punitive damages are unavailable under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act ... Thus, Mr. Hanna's request for punitive damages is stricken as to Count I." The demand letter (demand-letter-stadler-raines.docx.md, damages item 4) bases a $2,000,000 punitive-damages demand on "reckless disregard for Mr. Kovach's federally protected rights under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act." Its own Section V.A remedies paragraph lists only make-whole relief. A Texas Sabine Pilot claim might support punitive damages, but the letter ties the punitive demand to federal SOX rights. Two limits on the evidence: Hanna rests on the plaintiff's concession rather than a contested holding, and I did not separately confirm where the "reckless disregard of federally protected rights" phrasing comes from. Neither changes the conclusion, because the statute itself provides only make-whole relief.
